2119332592814067932.text:
i killed the infographics show with 1 claude opus prompt

now i made a full 10 minute story video in full code

this cost me $0 in ai video generations btw

turned it into a prompt you can use for free and make any topic u want, enjoy ↓

<inputs>
Ask me for my topic and my script. If I have no script, write one from my topic.
Ask which image model I have: GPT Image 2, or any model that takes reference images at 2K-4K, at about $0.03-0.05 an image.
Ask which voice I have: ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free.
Before generating everything, show me a look test: one plate, one character sheet cut out and rigged, and a 10 s shot with typing, a tag and a character who talks and points. Wait for my OK.
</inputs>

<look>
A 1920x1080 animated explainer in the style of the big flat-vector infographic channels.
- Every line of narration is acted out by cartoon people inside a full illustrated place.
- All motion is code. There are no AI video generations, just a few still images that code cuts up, rigs and animates.

Art:
- Flat colour shapes with NO outlines, at most one slightly darker flat shade for form, simple geometric shapes and crisp edges.
- Muted palette: dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple. Salmon-pink skin, big round heads, dot eyes, small bodies.
- Mood comes from the plate's own light: daylight, a cold blue night, warm indoor lamps.

Code colours:
- ink #2b2d42, red #d62828, orange #f4a261, gold #f6b93b, green #2fb37a, navy #1f2a48
- headline tomato #e2552f and purple #5b3fa6
- grey labels #8a8c9c, white cards #ffffff
- Font: Montserrat 800-900 (Google Fonts), all caps on cards and signs.

Pace:
- A new place every 3-4 s, about 10 places a minute.
- Something new arrives every 2 s: a tag, a stamp, a person walking in, a number.
- Never hold a still over 1 s. Never have a character who doesn't move.

Banned:
- outlines, glossy UI panels floating over the art, emoji, burned-in subtitles
- any channel's logo or name, photos of real people
- facts written on a plain colour card when the place could hold them
</look>

<art>
About 60 images in all ($2-3).

Every prompt starts with this style core, word for word:
"Flat vector illustration in exactly the same art style as the reference images: NO outlines or line art anywhere, every shape is a flat solid colour fill with at most one slightly darker flat shade for form, simple geometric shapes, crisp clean edges, no gradients, no texture, no painterly lighting. Muted modern palette: dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple, salmon-pink skin. No text, no letters, no numbers, no logos."

Then add one line that locks the setting ("The setting is [time, place]: [materials, light sources], nothing from other eras unless asked"). Feed 3-5 frames of a reference channel in as style references, with their logo cropped off.

1. Hero plates, about 24, one full 16:9 image each, for places you zoom into or come back to.
   - EMPTY: "no people, no characters, no animals".
   - Straight-on, with an open floor in the middle where characters will stand.
   - Blank signs, boards, screens and pages that code writes on later.
2. Quad plates, about 19, giving 76 more places. Pack 4 places into one image:
   "The image is a 2x2 grid of FOUR completely separate scenes, each filling exactly one quarter of the image (each quarter is itself a 16:9 picture), divided by perfectly straight thin pure-white gutters, one vertical down the exact centre and one horizontal across the exact centre."
   - Then describe the TOP-LEFT, TOP-RIGHT, BOTTOM-LEFT and BOTTOM-RIGHT scenes.
   - Split each quad on the brightest white row and column near the centre, walk out while the line stays over 60% white, and trim 6 px more.
   - Crop each tile to 16:9 at 1920x1080.
   - Object close-ups make great tiles: a desk, a screen, a document, a plate of food, a vault.
3. Main characters, 2-3 of them. Write one fixed description per character (age, hair, face, every piece of clothing with colours) and paste it word for word into every sheet.
   - Base sheet: 6 views. (1) front, neutral, drawn WITHOUT ARMS, only round smooth shoulder sockets where the arms would join; (2) the same armless front with a second emotion; (3) side view walking right; (4) seen from behind; (5) and (6) two poses the script needs.
   - Expression sheet: 6 armless fronts (hopeful, disgusted, terrified, exhausted, sick, shocked, or whatever the script needs), with the base sheet as a reference.
   - Pose sheet: 6 full poses with their props (sitting at a desk typing, sleeping, eating, running, signing, falling), with the base sheet as a reference.
4. Everyone else: role sheets of 4-6 people, each drawn in the exact pose their shot needs; crowd sheets of 8-10 small figures; prop sheets.
   - Every sheet: "on a solid flat chroma green background (#00B140) with lots of empty green space between figures; nothing touches, nothing on any character or object is green, full bodies, nothing cut off by the edges".
5. Thumbnail art: the same characters with richer saturated cartoon lighting and extreme emotions, the top quarter left free, no text, with the base sheets as references.
</art>

<rig>
Cutouts:
- The background is every border-connected pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40 and within 110 of the median green. Key only from the border, or dark clothes leak.
- Add a 2 px soft alpha band and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it, which kills the green fringe.
- Group the pieces by figure and drop specks. Name every sprite, and show me a named contact sheet.

Armless front figures become puppets:
- Split the head at the neck: the narrowest alpha row under the head.
- Find both shoulder sockets and the eye boxes.
- Inpaint the hole under the head from the body's own colours, so a nod never shows a gap.
- Write everything to rig.js: size, neck, sockets, eye boxes, skin RGB, sleeve RGB.
- Arms: upper L1 about 0.13 of the figure's height, lower L2 about 0.12, thickness about 0.04. Use sleeve colour to the elbow and skin for the forearm, a 0.82x darker sleeve when the arm is behind the body, and round caps and joins.
- Hands: mittens in three shapes (mitt, open, fist), plus a point with one finger out.
- Arm poses: each is a hand target relative to its shoulder, in units of L = L1 + L2, solved by two-bone IK (where there are two signs, the first is the left arm).
  - down: (∓0.04, 0.97)
  - rest: (±0.1, 0.9)
  - hips: (∓0.42, 0.55) with fists
  - point: right hand to (0.86, -0.32)
  - present: right hand to (0.75, 0.25), open
  - shrug: (∓0.62, 0.12), open
  - up: (∓0.32, -0.9)
  - hands on head
  - chin: a fist at the neck
  - hold: (±0.42, 0.45)
  - wave: (0.5, -0.75)
  - stop: (0.55, -0.1)
  - cheer: (∓0.55, -0.75) with fists
  - A pose change blends the two targets over 0.3-0.5 s with ease-in-out.
- Side, back and pose sprites stay whole images. Only the head turns, and a drawing or typing hand jitters ±6 px.
</rig>

<animation>
One HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time t: window .seek(t), READY, END, and EV, a list of sound events by name.
- Hang every shot on the narration: S('exact words', fn) starts a shot 0.08 s before that phrase. Repeated words are looked up by occurrence number.
- One function per shot, one shots file per chapter.

Motion primitives (Δ = t - start):
- pop: 0.3 s back-ease overshoot, 1 + 2.9(p-1)^3 + 1.9(p-1)^2.
- spring in: 1 - e^(-6.5Δ) cos(13Δ).
- kick on impact: 1 + 0.1 e^(-10Δ) cos(22Δ).
- shake: x = A e^(-8Δ) sin(61Δ), y = A e^(-8Δ) cos(47Δ).
- Exits shrink with ease-in over 0.25 s. Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a plain fade.

Camera:
- camP(plate, zoom, fx, fy) keeps the view inside the plate's edges.
- Every shot moves from one [zoom, fx, fy] to another with ease-in-out, a 2-4% push or a slow pan, so nothing holds still.
- Draw the plate and everything on it inside the same camera transform.
- Keep zoom under 1.33x on quad tiles. Zoom deeper only on hero plates.

Transitions:
- Push: the old shot slides out left while the new one slides in from the right, 0.24 s ease-in-out, with a whoosh 0.02 s before.
- Chapter splat: a #f4f1fb blob covers the screen in 0.2 s and clears in 0.2 s. It's a 1,250 px circle, 12 big satellite blobs at golden-angle spacing and 10 small droplets further out, shifted 120 px left on the way in and 140 px right on the way out.

Characters, alive in every frame:
- Breathing: scale 1 + 0.009 sin(2.3t).
- Head nod: 0.025 sin(2.1t) rad, or 0.025 sin(7t) + 0.02 sin(11.3t) while that character's line is spoken.
- Blink: every 2.7-4.2 s, seeded per figure. For 0.14 s, paint each eye box over in skin colour with a curved lash line.
- Walk:
  - Bob |sin| at 2.2% of the figure's height, with a body rock of ±0.035 rad.
  - Side-view walk sprites slide 1.5 leg lengths per step cycle, so the feet don't skate.
- Enter on the spring, sometimes with a hop. Fear is a fast shake (sin 70t). Surprise is a jump and an orange "!".
- A soft contact shadow ellipse under every figure. Night shots darken them with brightness(1 - k), so they match the plate.
- Every character on screen acts on its line: points at the thing being named, presents it, shrugs, cheers, holds its head.
</animation>

<graphics>
Text only lives on things in the world, typed letter by letter: 28 letters a second (34 for short tags). Each letter starts 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right and settles in 0.18 s with ease-out.

The full kit:
- Board: a white rounded board (radius 20) that drops 420 px on the spring and swings 0.25 rad into place, or stands on a wooden post and swings up from -1 rad.
  - Soft drop shadow (blur 22, y 8, 22%) and a faint darker strip along its bottom edge.
  - Lines typed 0.3 s apart.
- Date card: top left at (70, 70), white, 120 px tall, at least 330 px wide, radius 18. An orange calendar icon, a grey "DATE:" at 26 px, the date typed at 44 px weight 900. Pops in over 0.32 s.
- Place card: the same card with a red map pin and "PLACE:".
- Tag: a 6 px line with a dot at the thing, drawn in 0.2 s, then a rounded pill (the text at 40 px weight 900) pops on its end. Ink, red, gold or orange pills.
- Number card: a white card with a small grey label and a big red number. Long numbers roll up like a counter with ease-out.
- Red X: two round 30 px strokes, 0.11 s each, 0.01 s apart, with a soft shadow. One goes over every wrong idea.
- Stamp: red text in a double rounded border, tilted -0.12 rad. It slams from 2.1x to 1x in 0.14 s, then kicks.
- Banner: a full-width headline band, 92 px white caps on tomato or purple, rotated -0.02 rad, sliding in from the left over 0.22 s.
- Speech bubble: white, radius 36, with a tail. Thought cloud: a pill with two small circles.
- Orange "?" that bobs and sways over a puzzled head, and an orange "!" pop.
- White puff and poof clouds, speed lines, light blue sweat drops, coins and bills, a soft vignette, and a colour tint for mood.
- Write on the plate's own blank boards, screens and pages whenever the place has them. Measure the blank's rectangle on a grid overlay of the plate first.
</graphics>

<voice>
- ElevenLabs: a deep, warm US documentary narrator, eleven_v4, stability 0.5, similarity 0.75, style 0, speaker boost, with the timestamps endpoint.
- About 170-180 words a minute, using the voice's own speed setting (1.0-1.1). Never speed it up with atempo: it sounds chipmunked.
- Long scripts go in 3 chunks split at chapter breaks, passing the previous and next text so the read stays continuous.
- Cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, leave 0.5 s at chapter breaks, and add a 0.3 s lead-in.
- Rebuild word times from the alignment into words.js.
- Run faster-whisper over the result and diff it against the script before building the picture.
- Free route: Kokoro, then faster-whisper for the word times.
</voice>

<sound>
- Music: 2-3 free documentary beds from Pixabay, crossfaded over 3 s at big beats.
- Duck the music under the voice (30 ms attack, 0.3 s hold, 0.45 s release) and let it swell back up between chapters.
- SFX from Mixkit, one per event, aligned by their peaks, 6 dB quieter on speech: a typewriter tick on typing, a whoosh on pushes and splats, a pop on tags and cards, a thud on stamps, a hit on every red X, a ding on ticks, plus sounds that fit the scene.
- Gate: during speech the voice sits 15+ dB over music plus SFX (median of 100 ms frames), and the background is louder than the voice in under 1% of frames.
- Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1 dB.
</sound>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium or Edge, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, numpy. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Order:
   - the look test
   - the art in batches, with a contact sheet after each
   - cutouts and rig
   - voice and word times
   - shots, chapter by chapter
3. Check before any full render: a contact sheet per chapter, one frame every 2 s. Fix:
   - empty or overflowing signs
   - text over a face
   - black plate edges
   - feet floating off the floor
   - two shots in a row in the same place
   - any 4 s where nothing new arrives
4. Render at 30 fps, 4 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, frames piped to libx264 CRF 16-18.
   - Split long videos across 4-6 parallel browser pages and join the parts.
   - Scan the result for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Too few places reads as lazy. One plate held for 30 s with cards over it looks cheap. Budget about 10 new places a minute.
- Some image models ignore "no arms". GPT Image 2 follows it.
- Paste the same character description into every sheet and feed the base sheet back in, or faces and clothes drift.
- Quad tiles are only about 1920 px wide. Pushing past 1.33x looks soft.
- Plates with people already drawn in can't be animated. Ask for EMPTY and check before cutting.
- Text on a card floating over the art looks like a slideshow. Write on the world.
- Long renders crash. Render in parts you can rerun, and back up the shot files before every big patch.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, my script, my image model and my voice, then make the look test.
</start>

2119399547701014962.text:
Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.

But here's everything about Claude you must know:

Level 1. Don't be lazy, use the Claude desktop app.

You will still use the browser 90% of the time, and that's fine. But the day you start using the Claude desktop app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files one by one. You'd use Claude code more. There is no coming back from there.

Level 2. You have better things to do than spending 1 minute choosing the best model.

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. That's it.

Do not switch the models mid-chat. It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

Level 3. Either Medium or High effort. Nothing else

Medium when it is low-effort work. High for most of the tasks. But Extra High mostly burn through your usage limit.

Level 4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal and end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

Level 5. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

Level 6. Protect what you plug in.

Never click the thumbs up or down under an answer. You are basically giving feedback to AI, and they are allowed to send it to their training data. On a Team plan, once memory is on, leave it on: if an owner turns it off, every member’s memories are deleted permanently.

Your first 20 minutes, in order:

1. Install desktop app.
2. No settings are the best.
3. Connect ONE tool - not everything.
4. Use Claude Code more than you do.
5. Delete the installed skills, and add the new ones (written for the latest models)
6. Go to https://t.co/cn6xDN1uAS for my Claude skill library.

here is how we made this video, 100% in code.

1. Storyboard (Figma) 6 frames showing every stage: guide lines, dimensions, outline, fill, details, final icon.

2. Design to code (Figma MCP + Claude Code) Claude exported each frame as SVG, then a script split the finished icon into 15 layers for separate animation.

3. Animating the drawing (Remotion + React + SVG) Each layer has its own moment on the timeline. Lines draw themselves like someone's drafting them. Labels type in letter by letter with a caret. The fill resolves out of fine dots.

4. The camera (CSS 3D) The icon sits on a tilted plane, camera looking at it low, oblique, macro. Shallow depth of field keeps only the action sharp. A pool of light follows the action, everything else fades to black.

5. The edit (Remotion) 9 shots, hard cuts, camera always drifting toward the next action. The finale travels over the icon, pulls back, lands front-on and centred.

6. Revisions (Claude Code + Chrome previews) Everything 28% faster. Wider frame, softer shadow, whole numbers only on dimensions. Last frame is pixel-sharp, grain fades out.

7. Sound (Python + NumPy) Music generated from the film's own timings. Every on-screen event has its own sound. Tempo rises with the edit from 100 to 138 BPM, ends on a hit and a chord.

8. Render (Remotion + ffmpeg) 1080p, 60fps, motion blur, AAC audio at 320kbps. 31 seconds. 4 minute render.

2119536170946478504.text:
I love that people want to assume that I formed my opinions on the viability of current generation open-weight LLMs for enabling low-skilled criminals to find useful zero-day exploits, based on having just never used an LLM at all. 

The first thing I did when Anthropic added me to their CVP was build an autonomous zero-day exploitation pipeline. I've since backported it to use open-weight models because the token cost was insane, so I have a fairly good feel for both current frontier and open-weight model capabilities.

I'm well aware of what LLMs are capable of doing, and that they can, with the right steering or harness find zero-day exploits. Where we drift off course is with the claim that low-skilled criminals can just pick up something like GLM and find viable zero-day exploits.

I think that: 

a) More than 90% of CVEs are functionally useless for threat actors. Threat actors have a very specific operational needs and "random issue in random software" does not fall into their scope. 

b) Many (quite possibly even the majority of) critical rated CVEs are not exploitable under real-world conditions in a way that is useful to threat actors. There's entire teams in China dedicated to n-day exploitation and watching them will give you a good feel for what percent of critical RCEs are actually useful.

c) Threat actor with no exploit development background and minimal technical skills, even with access to a completely unrestricted open-weight LLMs, would struggle or completely fail to find useful zero-day exploits.

d) People with very little experience in software exploitation, Large Language Models, and CTI, are watching professional vulnerability researchers working with next-gen frontier models and ending up with a wildly unrealistic beliefs of just how "easy" what they are doing is.

e) There is an extremely noticeable lack of both zero-day exploitation and use of novel (non-public) n-day exploits by all threat actors, especially unskilled ones, and proponents of the "anyone can just pick up GLM and find useful zero-day exploits" theory continually refuse to even acknowledge that fact, let alone attempt to explain it.

I'm not coming at this from the position of some dude who just logs on to social media to says uninformed shit. I'm coming at this from the perspective of a researcher who has spent thousands of hours since LLMs came out researching their capabilities, and has also spent their entire career tracking threat actors and their capabilities. 

I have a mountain of real-world data, because the low-skilled AI-powered threat actors have a high tendency to accidentally infect themselves with their own malware. This often results in them exfiltrate their entire hard disk, along with all their AI prompt logs, to a vibe-coded C2 with client-side authentication (the admin credentials are hardcoded into the javascript or something equally stupid, so anyone can log in and download it).

My entire career I've been very pro "degrees and certs don't matter, everyone is welcome, and the best way to gain experience is hands-on practical work". But when I have some dude whose only experience is essentially just "downloaded abliterated GLM and scared himself with it", I feel like it's necessary to draw a line somewhere.

It's not just the bad opinions, everyone has bad opinions on something, I have plenty. It's that resources are actively being diverted away from addressing real and pressing issues in cybersecurity, as a result of FUD being spread about imaginary GLM-powered zero-day wielding scriptkiddies.

2119460293398937811.text:
I have been using Hermes Agent every day since day one, and I think it is finally time for a full review.

As always, this is completely independent. Not paid, not sponsored. The good and the bad, nothing held back.

This review covers what I use Hermes Agent for, why you should consider it, and how it stacks up against OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Bot.

Hermes has become essential for me. Let me show you why, starting with the first thing most of you asked.

Which models do I use inside Hermes?

The best thing about Hermes is that it is truly model-neutral. It does not degrade the models. Whatever a model can do, you get directly.

I use GLM 5.3 a lot, and for light and medium tasks it is excellent. Sometimes I switch to GPT Sol 6.1, and I have noticed that the best place to run GPT is Hermes, even better than Codex. I have tried a lot of models in Hermes, and they were all excellent.

So use any model that suits you, as long as the plan is generous, and run two or three at once if you want. Here is the important part: in ninety percent of use cases, your choice of model will not make a big difference. The model here is still just a brain behind bigger layers, and those layers are what control how it behaves.

Usage limits and cost

There is no Hermes quota. Plug in your key, run a local model, or subscribe through Nous Portal. That is all it takes.

You can push Hermes to the max with excellent models without paying a single dollar. And if you decide to pay, you get great value for it.

Caching is great too

Out of 1,013 sessions, here's one that came out right at the average:

219 million input tokens
15.7 million output tokens
3.77 billion cached tokens
About 4 billion tokens in total

94.4% from cache.

Hermes is one of the best I have used for token efficiency, and the transparency is total. While you work, you see the real speed of every provider and every detail.

Light on the machine

Hermes is not heavy at all. One day I set up a full Hermes agent inside a virtual machine with just 2 GB of RAM, and it ran with very high stability on every kind of task I gave it. That shocked me. Codex, for comparison, eats tens of gigabytes of RAM. That difference tells you what an engineering masterpiece Hermes Agent is.

The layer above the model

One of the biggest things that sets Hermes apart is that the agent is separate from its brain. The model is the brain, and you can swap it without losing your memory, your skills or your setup.

Anywhere else, when I use GLM 5.3 I get GLM's usual strengths and weaknesses, and when I use Sol 6.1 I get Sol's. In Hermes there is a layer above the model that gives it a soul, a style and an understanding of how I work, so switching models matters far less. At some point the models feel eighty percent alike in style, in method and in the things you care about. What is left is raw capability, so the most capable models go to the hardest problems.

You own the layer you actually invest your time in. And the beautiful part is that this layer, the identity, the memory, the skills and every tool, is completely mine.

Look at Claude Code getting people banned today, at model performance suddenly dropping, at Codex being stingy with usage one time and slow the next. Those are constraints, and Hermes does not have them. If Claude Code decides to change or remove something, you have no say. In Hermes you can always change whatever you want. That is sovereignty, freedom and empowerment.

Memory that grows with you

When I opened the skills and memory tree, I found that Hermes had reached the point where it knows me better than any other agent. It grew with me through this whole journey, and that is what makes it the ideal partner for my work.

The journey command shows you a star map of your memory and skills, and you can edit or delete anything in it. It is one of the greatest things in Hermes.

One example: when Fable came out I loved it, so I had Fable pass its style and way of thinking on to Hermes. My Hermes became twice as useful after that.

And the instructions stick. Across sessions and updates, the soul, the identity and the instructions are always there. I never feel I need to remind it, and I never notice it forgetting or drifting. It is with me one hundred percent, every time.

Research and academic writing

Hermes is excellent for research and academic writing. With Claude Code or Codex I always have to explain my method, my way of thinking and everything I do not want. In Hermes I explained myself once, and from then on research and writing just happen the way I want. You set it up once, and it keeps growing. It even picked up my taste in design and research.

Skills and tools

Hermes has skills and tools you will not find anywhere else, and the team never stops building. The skills library is one of the best I have seen.

I see about 165 skills built in, plus optional skills and plugins you can add with one click. All useful stuff for growing in any field: iOS apps, computer use, automation, shopping, coding, organization, security, travel, testing, data, streaming, support, sports, reviews, video and more.

The tools cover web search, the browser, the terminal, files, vision, image generation, subagents, scheduled tasks, memory and computer use, and MCP brings in anything else. You can use it with Blender or whatever you want. Use it straight out of the box, or customize it with no ceiling.

Where I talk to it

You can talk to it anywhere: iMessage, Telegram, Slack, Discord and more, and you can customize all of it. When I am out of the house, Hermes is the first thing I think of. I send it a message and everything happens like magic.

My own voice model

Companies that take speech-to-text out of your credits always annoyed me. In Hermes I brought my own model. Everything runs locally on my machine, smooth and fast, exactly the way I want. I even send it voice notes on Telegram, and it just works.

The desktop app

The desktop app is great, and the user experience is one of the best I have seen. I do not like working in the terminal in general, so in Hermes the desktop app is my home.

What I use it for

The idea that Hermes is only for casual users or simple tasks is just not true. It works for every kind of use and then some. I use it for everything I want, and I get great results.

It is the agent I rely on for personal tasks, light work and organization. The test videos and model comparisons I publish are edited entirely by Hermes; I do not touch them. It has helped me study and work, proofread academic research, translate books and documents, run a security audit on my ERP application, and a lot more.

Hermes vs OpenClaw

The most unfair comparison people make is Hermes vs OpenClaw. OpenClaw was a revolution in its time and started a huge wave, and it deserves credit for that. But it is nowhere near Hermes. Not in stability, not in reliability, not in consistency, not in capability. To me, OpenClaw is a tool some people enjoy for two or three days of experimenting. Is it something you can rely on and build projects, ideas and solutions on? Not at all.

Hermes is another story. It even beats tools like Claude Code and Codex. For me it sits in a different category entirely.

Hermes vs Claude Code and Codex

The reply I get most is: you can do all of this in Claude Code or Codex. Yes, you can. But in Hermes I do it the way I want, not the way the model or the company wants, and I enjoy the work instead of fighting the agent.

Hermes also refuses less than any agent I use, and that matters a lot to me. It is my first stop for anything that usually gets refused in Claude Code, Codex and the rest. A while ago I gave Claude Code and Codex a task and both refused. Hermes did it.

Hermes vs Grok Bot

Grok Bot has two real advantages. It works out of the box and it is easy, and it has direct access to X. Beyond that, Hermes crushes it.

Everyone is talking about how fast Grok Bot's quotas run out, and I can confirm it. I am on the Ultra plan, the $200 one, and it does not last me more than a day, two, maybe three. That is not sustainable. To be fair, usage limits are a problem with a lot of providers right now, not only Grok Bot.

The real difference is intelligence. Grok Bot is extremely low on intelligence right now. I ask it to execute a task and it just answers. I ask it a question and it starts executing. I cannot trust it. Its mistakes outnumber its wins, and it keeps telling me it cannot do this, it cannot reach that, this is a limit.

In Hermes, you shape the intelligence layer. I shaped mine to do nothing until it is sure what I want and has reviewed every detail and the full context. Grok Bot has nothing like that, and you cannot shape it. Believe me, I tried.

Do not confuse ease with quality. Grok Bot has a wonderful ecosystem, great templates and amazing growth. But you do not own the environment, you do not choose the kind of intelligence you get, and you struggle to make it through the week.

The problems

Hermes is not perfect, and you should know where it falls short.

Sometimes when I change the model in a session, the interface does not show it. The change happens; the UI just does not read it. Open a new session, come back, and you will see it was applied.

Steering is hit or miss. Sometimes a steering message redirects the conversation right away. But most of the time the agent ignores it completely and waits until the whole task is done, or it spends a really long time on the task before the steering finally kicks in. I always wish steering was instant so no time gets wasted.

Subagents are excellent, but sometimes Hermes hands me a result and then waits for the subagent's report, instead of waiting first and giving me one final result.

Computer use is one of the most important features for me, and it sometimes breaks and needs a real fix. It happened enough that I stopped using it heavily. It usually breaks under heavy work or with medium and weaker models, so give it your most capable models.

That brings me to the most dangerous problem. Weaker models can wreck your Hermes in minutes. You build your setup and the agent's understanding of you with a serious model, then a weak model starts making bad decisions and damages that whole layer. It can even break the app. MiniMax M3 broke my Hermes more than once with its hallucinations.

The fix is simple: stick to the leading, stable models, such as Kimi, Sol, GLM 5.3, DeepSeek Flash, and frontier Qwen models like Qwen 3.8 Max, and stay away from weak, hallucinating ones. Since I stopped using MiniMax M3, I have not hit this once. I do not know if it has been fixed, but I am not risking my stability to find out. What I really want is an optional protection layer for the memory, the soul file and AGENTS.md, so any edit shows up in the interface for me to approve first.

Long tasks can occasionally collapse in goal mode. The agent marks the task done before it is, or gets lost and loops. That happened a long time ago and has not happened since. It is rare and usually comes with weaker models, but I am mentioning it for transparency.

One for Mac users: more than once, an update left my desktop app stuck on an older version. The fix is simple. Quit the app and run hermes update in the terminal. If the app still shows the old version, run hermes desktop to rebuild it.

What I want next

Two things matter most to me.

First, a solid, easy mobile app with beautiful interfaces and that Nous spirit.

Second, an easy mode that works out of the box: add profiles by field, so a researcher, a programmer, or a writer starts from a ready base instead of a raw zero.

A model from Nous Research that understands Hermes better than any other model would be amazing too, but that is not central for me right now.

And I want Hermes to switch modes from natural language. When I give it a goal, it should turn on goal mode by itself and finish the whole task, the way Codex and sometimes Claude Code do.

The community and the team

One moment made me appreciate Hermes more than ever. I wanted Arabic support in the harnesses I use, so I reached out to MiniMax, Zai and others and offered to translate the harness, the website, everything, myself. They all said yes. Then nothing happened.

With Hermes, I did the Arabic localization myself and opened a pull request. They accepted it, and today Hermes speaks Arabic. Your voice as a user is what matters, and that is exactly why I love Hermes.

Another thing that amazed me: one day I sent the team an idea right here on X. I wished I could set the model for each scheduled task. In less than three hours it was built and shipped, and I have been using it ever since. I have never seen that kind of speed. That is what accelerating growth looks like when a project is open source and the whole community builds it.

Where I stand

I have tried most of the well-known tools in the space, and every tool has beautiful positives and annoying negatives. Hermes might be the one with the fewest negatives. Not because it is better or worse than the others, but because in Hermes you can deal with a negative, change it, erase it, and sometimes turn it into a strength. It all comes down to how you customize it.

It is not the easiest tool to start with, so my next post is my full setup, as a skill. Hand it to your agent, answer its questions, and it sets everything up for you. I do not claim it is the best setup, only the one that fits me. Stay tuned!

After all this time, I know exactly where I stand. Hermes is a victory for what open source is supposed to mean.

Ask me for: one topic as a "what if" question (default: "What if the Sun vanished?"), the length (default 30 seconds), and whether I have an ElevenLabs key (if not, use a free local voice).
</inputs>

<direction>
A Kurzgesagt-style animated explainer at 1920x1080, 30fps, drawn entirely in code: one 2D canvas plus one WebGL canvas for planets.
Space: a vertical gradient #081d2c to #102348, five huge parallax nebula blobs (teal rgb 24,150,160 at 20%, blue 40,95,195 at 16%, coral 220,95,110 at 10%, indigo 60,70,175 at 15%), three star layers at parallax depths .12/.35/.6 that twinkle, 40% of the near stars drawn as 4-point sparkles.
The Sun: radius 300px, half off the left edge. A radial gradient #fff7dc to #ffc857 to #ff8f4a with an offset highlight, additive halo rings at 1.23/1.48/1.76/2.1x the radius, 18 faint rotating ray wedges, 28 drifting glowing granules on its surface.
Earth: an orthographic sphere in a fragment shader, 4x supersampled, from a 2048x1024 map painted from longitude/latitude polygons: land #5fc47a, forest #48ad6b, desert #f5c75f, rainforest #3a9d62, ice #f1f8ff, ocean gradient #4dc7eb to #1a66b8, white capsule clouds. Tilt .26 rad, spin .55 degrees per second. Day/night uses smoothstep(-.12, .24, N·L) with the light direction recomputed from Sun to Earth every frame. Navy night side with ~380 warm city lights, a coral band on the terminator, a cyan rim, ocean specular, an atmosphere halo that is stronger on the lit side.
A small astronaut mascot (~180px) built from rounded rectangles: suit #f3f7fb, orange #ff8f4a boots, a visor gradient #1f5a73 to #0a1c2c with glowing cyan eyes that look at whatever matters, a blinking antenna light, an idle bob, squash and stretch on every pose.
Type: Fredoka 600/700 only. Captions in caps with 3-6px letter spacing in teal #8fd8e6, gold #ffd98a or white, sitting in rounded pills of rgb(6,20,40) at 62%. Every line of text rises 1.3x its own height through a clip on an ease-out-quint.
Finish: a vignette to rgba(4,4,20,.45) and a 6% film grain re-randomized 24 times per second.
Banned: outlines, flares or loops on the Sun's edge, static infographic strips, full stops in on-screen text, text that fades in whole, AI images or AI video, Kurzgesagt's own characters, bird or music.
</direction>

<structure>
30 seconds, every line of narration gets a camera move or a transformation, nothing ever holds still.
Tight on the Sun at 2.25x (0s) → on the word "vanished" it swells 6% for 0.22s, collapses in 0.33s, then a white flash and a shockwave ring (1s) → pull back to 1x revealing Earth still lit and the astronaut staring at the empty spot (1.6-3s) → on "eight" an 8:20 countdown slams in from 1.7x to 1x and starts ticking, a "LAST LIGHT" label rides the edge of the growing dark disc (3.2s) → dive to 2.3x on Earth with light streaks flowing in (5.6s) → on "you" a YOU pin drops (7s) → on "left" a photon lands on the pin with "THIS LIGHT LEFT THE SUN / 8 MIN 20 SEC AGO" (7.5s) → on "play" the pin morphs into a play button, "YOU PRESSED PLAY / 15 SEC AGO" (8.8s) → one pull-back from 2.4x to a 0.3x orbit view, "LAST LIGHT" and "GRAVITY" riding the ring (9.6-12.5s) → on "nothing" a dotted circle at the empty centre (13.4s) → on "hits" the darkness sweeps Earth in 0.7s, city lights pop on, the countdown turns gold at 0:00 (15.8s) → on "black" the background fades almost to black (17.4s) → Jupiter appears, "STILL SHINING FOR 1 HOUR+" (17.9s) → zoom out, a dashed tangent line, "30 KM/S" as Earth flies straight off (20.8s) → a thermometer counts 15 to -70°C while frost grows from the poles (22.8s) → a 0.8s rewind on a separate story clock (24.3s) → sunglasses drop onto the astronaut (25.2s) → a photon tagged "8:20 OLD", then the title (27.7s).
For any other topic, keep the same shape: the event happens on its word, pull back to show scale, dive in to make it personal ("you"), pull back out, the consequence with a live counter, an escalation, a funny beat with the mascot, a callback and the title.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file. Every frame is a pure function of time: https://t.co/cTZzFgqbdH(t) draws frame t. No timers, no CSS animation.
2. Camera moves on easeInOutCubic, zoom is interpolated in log space, every pop is a damped spring (damping .42-.5, frequency 12-16).
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with a designed voice (calm, warm, curious male, late 30s, crisp, light neutral European English), stability .5, similarity .75, generated with timestamps. Without a key, use kokoro-onnx locally and get word times with faster-whisper. Every animation event fires on its word. About 165 words per minute, 0.24s between sentences, a 0.36s beat before the big reveal.
4. The darkness front: any pixel within the front's radius from the Sun turns to night with a 30px soft edge. The front moves at ~47px/s and ramps to 700px/s near Earth.
5. Keep two clocks: ambient time for twinkle, spin and bob, and a separate story clock for events, so a rewind stays consistent.
6. Render with Playwright in headless Edge with the GPU: seek every frame at 30fps and blend 2 subframes (shutter 0.6) for motion blur, then encode with libx264 at CRF 16 for the master and CRF 20 for delivery.
7. Sound: a calm royalty-free space music bed 7dB under the voice, timed so its natural ending lands on the title, swelling 5dB under the title. One downloaded royalty-free sound effect per event kind (collapse, impact, pull-back whoosh, countdown tick, dive, pin tap, photon land, play click, light hit, reveal, frost, rewind), each peak-aligned to its frame and 4-10dB under the voice. Master with gain plus a limiter to -14 LUFS, -2.2dB true peak.
</build>

<gotchas>
Make the WebGL globe canvas at least 2 x radius x zoom x 1.18 pixels or the sphere clips flat in close-ups. Never draw prominences on the Sun's edge, they read as white hooks. Never pad the voice to fit the visuals, tighten the read instead. Speed the darkness front up near Earth or it takes 13 seconds to cross the planet. Show me a contact sheet of every beat before rendering.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me the inputs, write the narration with the beat each word triggers, show it to me, then build and render the video.
</start>

The answer is no. My harness has absolutely nothing to do with T3 Code. For starters T3 Code is not a harness.

T3 Code and others alike drives other agents. It doesn't run one itself. For example, Codex, Claude Code, or others, they do the actual work underneath.

A better comparision would be DeepSeek Harness.

My harness talks straight to the model API and runs everything itself: the loop, the tools, context and compaction, and the check for when a task is actually done. Point it at a model endpoint, and it works.

So yes, it's a full blown harness.

2119823616774992084.text:
In 2015, I built an AI that detects early cancer.

It’s still running across hundreds of hospitals in the US today.

It was the most fulfilling work of my life, and I was building in AI years before everyone called it “AI”.

Building in AI then was a dream.

Now It feels like we’ve taken a turn for the worse.

It started when i was in undergrad.

I built my first company: AI models that made the political data transparent to voters.

At 21, I was offered six figures for it, but the buyers wanted to use it for reasons I couldn't ethically support.

So we turned down the offer and shut down the company instead.

In 2014, I moved into deep learning research on language models, for the Intelligence Community and Goldman Sachs.

Then HCA Healthcare came to us.

They put me in a competition against 10 people from IBM Watson. It was just me and the tools I’d built.

Our job was to build an AI model that can catch the cancer that slips through the cracks in hospitals.

It was the most intense 30 days of my life. Multiple all nighters.

My models won. That turned into a $5M deal, and later its own company, Azra AI.

Then the world caught on.

ChatGPT and Claude arrived, and AI costs exploded.

Building in AI in 2015 felt novel.

We were using it to find cancer tumours and save lives.

Now the biggest tech companies have turned AI into a money extraction machine.

That’s when I decided to make a change.

We raised $8.5M to build a better future for AI.

On Wednesday, we’re launching Rayline.

AI shouldn’t be locked inside a few labs’ models, prices and clouds. It should be open, transparent and decentralized.

More on Wednesday.

Prompt:
PURPLE POWER AWAKENING — POST-APOCALYPTIC BIKER BAR FIGHT

A 30-second horizontal 16:9 photorealistic supernatural action scene. Five adult bikers humiliate a young woman on the floor of a rusted wasteland bar, until violet energy erupts from her hands and she takes all five of them down in one continuous fight. It ends with her walking alone out of the open door into the dusk dust storm while every biker lies knocked out on the floor behind her.

MAIN SUBJECT
The woman from Image1, an adult in her early twenties, East Asian, with dark brown eyes and a calm, cool face. Hair: a choppy chin-length bob in a gradient from hot pink at the roots to violet and bright blue at the tips, with ONE small silver lightning-bolt hair clip on the left side. Outfit: a fitted pink-and-white sports crop top with white stripes across the chest; a pink pleated mini skirt with white inner pleats and two white stripes along the hem, with matching pink fitted shorts underneath; a pink backpack strapped tightly to her back with black buckle straps that never comes off. Footwear: knee-high glossy black combat boots on chunky pink platform soles, with pink straps, silver studs, buckles and metal rings. All fabric is dense and opaque and stays in place during every jump and strike, even when soaked. Athletic, toned build with subtle muscle definition. At first her expression is exhausted and frightened; after the awakening it becomes cold, fierce and focused. During the fight her hands and forearms are wrapped in glowing violet-purple energy. Preserve her face, hair colour, outfit and boots EXACTLY as in Image1 in every shot.

THE BIKERS (FIVE adult men, each keeps his own look in every shot)
- BIKER 1: lean, short bleached-blond mohawk, black leather vest with patches over a bare chest, fingerless gloves.
- BIKER 2: large and stocky, shaved head, thick brown beard, sleeveless denim vest, holds a dented STEEL bucket filled with water only.
- BIKER 3: tall and thin, round welding goggles pushed up on his forehead, brown leather jacket.
- BIKER 4: dark curly hair, oil-stained grey tank top, black leather vest.
- BIKER 5: long greasy black hair under a red bandana, studded leather jacket.
All bikers wear worn jeans and heavy black boots. The only object any biker holds is BIKER 2's steel bucket; no other weapons.

LOCATION AND HEIGHT
A ground-level post-apocalyptic bar built from scrap. Ceiling height is 3.5 metres, made of corrugated rusted metal sheets on wooden beams. Walls are rusted corrugated metal patched with plywood and old road signs with no readable text. Floor is cracked grey concrete covered in dust and sand.
Foreground: oil-drum tables, scattered sand, broken glass on the floor.
Midground: a long bar counter of weathered dark wood with dusty beer bottles on scrap-metal shelves, and one elderly bartender who ducks behind the counter when the awakening starts and stays hidden there.
Background: a wide open metal door on the far wall. Outside is a wasteland at dusk in a slow-moving dust storm, dim brownish-orange and darker than the bar interior; it adds no light to the room but stays visible in every wide shot.
Moving details: dust drifting in the lamp light, lamps swaying slightly on their cords, sand blowing in through the open door.

CAMERA AND LOOK
Photorealistic live-action action-film cinematography with real stunt choreography. ONE light source for the whole video: FIVE bare tungsten bulbs hanging on cords from the ceiling, giving warm orange light from above, soft dusty haze, natural skin tones and muted contrast. The only other light is the violet glow of her energy, which reflects on her face, the metal walls, the wet floor near the wall and the bikers' leather. Her pink outfit and pink-blue hair stay the brightest colours in the warm bar. Camera defects: handheld shake, slight delayed autofocus on fast moves, mild bloom on the bulbs, faint film noise. Regular shots last 1.5-2.5 seconds, and every cut comes after a completed movement; the bucket jump is ONE continuous shot. The camera and crew never appear in frame. No glossy beauty lighting, no artificial rim light, no heavy colour grading.

CONTINUOUS STORY

00:00-00:06 — HUMILIATION
Start in motion: low-angle shot at floor level. Two bikers pull her by the arms across the dusty concrete, their heavy boots stepping beside her while her black-and-pink platform boots scrape along the floor; they let go and she slides to a stop sitting against the corrugated metal wall, backpack against the wall. Cut to a high close-up: BIKER 2 tips the dented steel bucket over her, a stream of cold water pours over her head and shoulders, and her wet pink-to-blue hair sticks to her face. Cut to a low wide shot from her eye level on the floor: all FIVE bikers stand over her in a half circle, laughing, BIKER 2 holding the now empty bucket, with the bar counter and the open door with the dust storm visible behind them.

00:06-00:10 — POWER AWAKENS
Close-up: still sitting, she slowly lifts her head and looks up through her wet pink hair with a cold, fierce stare; the silver lightning clip catches the light. Thick violet-purple smoke and crackling electric arcs coil around both hands and forearms, and a purple glow lights up the wet concrete under her palms. Cut to a low wide shot: she presses ONE palm to the floor and a violet shockwave bursts outward across the floor, throwing up dust and sand. All FIVE bikers lose their balance and stumble backward, the hanging bulbs swing, and the bartender ducks behind the counter. She pushes off the floor and rises to her feet in a low fighting stance.

00:10-00:16 — FIRST PUNCH
She dashes at BIKER 1, her platform boots pounding the concrete. Tight close-up of ONE clear contact: her right fist, wrapped in violet arcs, hits his face, and a purple flash bursts at the moment of impact. His head snaps back, his short mohawk trembles and his face twists from the shock. She immediately follows with a second strike to his chest, leaving a trail of violet smoke and glowing particles behind her arm while her bob swings with the motion. He flies backward, crashes onto an oil-drum table, rolls over it and drops to the floor.

00:16-00:21 — THE BUCKET (ONE continuous wide shot)
BIKER 2 charges at her, swinging the empty steel bucket overhead. Take-off: she pushes off the floor with both platform boots. Flight: she leaps forward, knees tucked, skirt and shorts staying in place, backpack tight on her back, violet energy flaring around her fists. Contact: her glowing fist hits the bucket in an upward strike; the bucket is torn out of his hands, flies straight up and smashes into the corrugated metal ceiling 3.5 metres above, denting it and bringing down rust flakes, dust and loose pieces of sheet metal. The violet burst from the same strike throws BIKER 2 backward into the bar counter; bottles fall and shatter, and he slides down to the floor. Landing: she lands in a crouch on both boots, knees bent, as debris falls around her.

00:21-00:26 — TWO AT ONCE
Medium-wide shot: BIKER 3 and BIKER 4 rush at her from opposite sides. She blocks BIKER 3's swinging arm with her left forearm, pivots on her platform boot, and drives a glowing violet palm into BIKER 4's chest, with purple light spreading across his tank top on impact. He falls backward. She turns back and hits BIKER 3 in the jaw with a violet punch, and his goggles fly off his forehead. He spins and falls face-down onto the concrete. ONE clear contact per strike, readable choreography, real body weight and recoil.

00:26-00:30 — FINISH AND EXIT
BIKER 5 runs for the open door. She catches him from behind in two steps, pulls him down and slams him onto his back a few metres from the door. Low close-up from the floor: she kneels over him, wet pink-blue hair hanging around her face, a dense sphere of violet energy crackling in her raised hand, and dark cracks with glowing purple veins spread across the concrete around his head. She closes her hand and the sphere fades. Final wide shot from behind: she stands up, steps over him and walks slowly toward the open door, pink backpack and platform boots clearly visible, with all FIVE bikers knocked out around her, weakly stirring and groaning, among broken bottles, under the dented ceiling and swinging bulbs. The frame ends with her standing in the doorway, lit from above by the bulbs, facing the dim dusk dust storm.

SOUND
Natural and event-driven only: boots scraping on concrete during the drag; the splash of water hitting her and the floor; the bikers' rough laughter, which cuts off at the awakening; a deep rumbling hum and electric crackle around her hands; the low boom of the shockwave and sand hissing across the floor; heavy platform-boot steps on concrete; heavy punch impacts with a short electric snap on each violet hit; the oil-drum table crashing; the steel bucket clanging into the metal ceiling and debris rattling down; bottles shattering; bodies hitting concrete; her heavy breathing; low groans of the bikers and wind with sand from the open door at the end. No music, no narration, no laugh track.

ESSENTIAL CONTINUITY
- The story goes in strict order: drag, bucket of water, awakening, Biker 1, Biker 2, Bikers 3 and 4, Biker 5, exit. Each biker is defeated ONCE and stays down.
- FIVE bikers total, each keeps his own hair, face and clothing in every shot; no new bikers appear. The bartender stays hidden behind the counter after the awakening.
- Her look never changes: pink-to-violet-to-blue bob, ONE silver lightning clip, pink-and-white sports crop top, pink pleated mini skirt with white stripes and pink shorts underneath, pink backpack with black buckle straps, black-and-pink platform combat boots. Her hair stays pink-violet-blue and is never recoloured by the energy.
- The bucket holds only water, no ice, is empty after 00:06, is the same dented steel bucket throughout, hits the ceiling ONCE, and the ceiling dent remains visible afterwards.
- The jump has take-off, flight and landing; no body passes through tables, the counter or other people; she steps over Biker 5, not through him.
- Violet energy appears only on her hands and forearms, plus the shockwave, the floor cracks and the final sphere; it is always violet-purple.
- The same bar layout, the same hanging-bulb lighting, and the open door with the dim dusk dust storm stay in the background; no daylight enters the room.
- Preserve her face, hair, outfit and footwear exactly as in Image1 throughout.

No repeated attempts, slow motion, teleportation, duplicated people, changing outfits, changing hair colour, lost backpack, changing faces, extra limbs, distorted hands, weapons other than the steel bucket, guns, blood, gore, ice cubes, cartoon or anime style, CGI appearance, captions, subtitles, readable signs, watermarks, recording interface.

Seele is a company that creates AI tools for game making. Recently they invited me to participate as they took on a 5-day challenge to push their new model, Seele03, to its limits and move closer and closer to AAA with a Wuxia-style action game.

The product consists of their AI model, asset generators, and target engines such as web (three.js), Unity, or even Unreal. What's nice is that their site has everything in one place, from mesh generators and rigging to sound fx and sprite work. They also provide common templates for most types of games. Having it all work together seamlessly saves a lot of time. You can get a game running very quickly, in 20 minutes or so. (20 minutes! I remember when this took months and months.)

So what can they do in 5 days?

Their progress video, below, shows them iterating through creating a Phantom Blade Zero-style game. This is not reverse engineering, but made from scratch. Over the course of development, they sent me video updates on their progress. The 03 model is designed for iterative development, and I gave them some advice as they took it from basically nothing to the final version of the video today. The progress the model made day to day was rapid, and the traces actually factored in something that I don't see that often: game design.

Most models focus on the graphics when making a game, but Seele03 is thinking about combos, hit feedback, everything that really matters for how a game feels and plays. One day, I think that's going to be the core of what makes AI game making viable.

After you are done prompting and refining your game, it's not frozen on the web. You can download and edit the project files themselves. Since you can download the result and open it in Godot or Unity (Unreal is embedded web atm), Seele03 can give you a quality core and a way for you to take things even further.

So how did it turn out? I've tried a lot of game generators, and Seele03's all-in-one tool approach and engine targeting stand out for me. Most others only generate three.js for web, or are more world models based on generative rendering. This is the rare one I've seen that is making games directly in game engines.

They've asked me to share the full process video with you so you can judge for yourself. As I watched the team work, I sat back and wondered at how it's all changing so fast: you simply... chat... interacting with a UI that is purely text, typing in wishes and directions, and everything else unfolds around you. I think they got pretty far in their goal gameplay-wise, which is where they really focused. The key thing is that after you have the final result, you also have the files to download, and you can replace anything you want to take it even further: animations, level graphics, basically anything.

Ramp, a $60B company, hid a secret offer on its website that only AI could see.

in 32 days, AI told buyers about it 370 times.

here's the genius AEO experiment behind it:

1. They built a second version of their site just for AI

- Ramp put an offer on about 50 pages that only AI bots could see
- Human visitors saw nothing different
- Then they tracked whether ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity would pass the offer on to real buyers

2. They tested 3 formats to see what AI actually reads

- Markdown
- Plain stripped down HTML
- Pages packed with schema, the code made for machines
- Everyone expected schema to win
- Markdown was the only format that reliably showed up in AI answers

3. They found out who was really visiting their site

- Thousands of visits from 7 different AI platforms in just 2 weeks
- Some AI bots pretend to be normal browsers. DeepSeek shows up as a Chrome version from 2017
- Claude's crawler visited more than all the other named AI crawlers combined

4. They asked the AI tools buyer questions every single day

- The same questions a CFO would ask when picking a spend management tool
- Then they checked every answer for their offer

5. Every AI behaved completely differently

- Claude passed on the exact offer, the link and step-by-step instructions
- Perplexity only mentioned it vaguely
- ChatGPT read the pages but mentioned the offer 0 times in 32 days
- One strategy for "AI" doesn't work. Each model needs its own plan

6. The biggest lesson: AI trusts pages it already cites

- Pages that AI was already citing were the ones where the offer showed up
- Pages with few AI citations got zero mentions, whatever the format
- One of the best pages was one Ramp never cared about for Google

the result:

- 1,300+ AI bot visits in the first 2.5 weeks
- about 40 AI answers mentioning the offer at 2.5 weeks
- 370 by day 32, almost 10x
- a peak of 33 in a single day

Ramp didn't win this by writing more blogs

they figured out which pages AI already trusts, then put the right message there

and that's the whole game now: if AI doesn't already trust the pages talking about you, it won't recommend you.

if you want to know which pages ChatGPT and Claude trust in your niche, and get your brand mentioned on them.

F*ck it im leaking everything 

Here is exactly how these videos are made and what every tool does 

Step 1 : Pick the story and write the script

-> You give claude a story / idea for a video 

Step 2 : Make the voiceover

-> Claude asks for your elevenlabs api key and turns it into a voiceover 
-> FFmpeg is a free video and audio tool run from the command line claude uses it to speed up the voice and reduce silences and cuts 

Step 3 : Time every word

-> Claude uses Whisper it is a free speech-to-text that listens to the voiceover and records the exact moment each word is spoken everything else is timed to these word times 

Step 4 : Design the characters

-> Claude uses an HTML canvas and Javascript to draw the character with code (circles, lines, colours) its not an AI image generator Every pose and expression (grin, shock, pointing) is saved as a flat cutout picture in HTML 

Step 5: Plan every frame

-> Claude uses Three.js to plan out a camera path for the video three.js is a 3D engine that runs in a web browser but i just use it to figure out where the camera goes and where each character stands 

Step 6: Build the 3D world

-> A Python script builds every set in Blender from simple shapes , It adds cartoon lighting and a dark outline on everything so the world matches the characters Props like coins, sparks, confetti and the car are real 3D objects

Step 7: Render the frames 

-> Claude uses EEVEE renderer on YOUR GPU and Blender goes through the plan frame by frame, places the camera and the character cutouts inside the 3D world, and saves each frame as an image This is the slow part the render time depends on your GPU

Step 8: Make the sound

-> Claude uses FREE websites like Mixkit/Pixabay  which adds real sound effects on the exact frames where things happen 

Step 9: Captions 

-> Python turns the word times from Whisper into bold captions that show one or two words at a time 

Step 10: Put it all together 

-> Claude uses FFmpeg to joins all the frames into one video it adds a soft glow, burns in the captions and adds the sound mix 

Step 11: One click

-> Instead of claude doing step 5,7,10 on its cloud and burning your usage it insteads sends a windows batch (.bat) file to your pc and you run those steps locally

I hear this all the time.

Then I meet people like Ryan Mathews who vibe coded an elk call app to $650K annual run rate in 110 days with Claude Code.

The wildest part to me is how his marketing came together (pretty much by accident):

-He recorded a 45-minute video designed to be a Meta ad then decided to post it to YouTube. He expected ~2k views but it got 150k.

-When his first Meta campaigns weren’t converting, he told Meta to find people who’d watch 75% of that 45-minute video. It cost about $1.50 per person to watch 35 minutes. He was making $2 back for every $1 from the start.

-He launched a “retargeting” campaign that crushed the main one. Then he went to record a Loom for a client and noticed he never saved the targeting. This led him to realize that cold traffic sent straight to the landing page beat the warm-up video in terms of ROAS.

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.

Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

a number of respected researchers (e.g. @DKokotajlo @bshlgrs @ajeya_cotra @RyanGreenblatt)  have suggested that the METR-documented ~2x speedup in AI progress at anthropic over the last year supports the hypothesis that there will be a near-term (e.g. 2027) intelligence explosion (IE). how exactly does this reasoning work?

one way to think about this: perhaps the leading alternative to the near-term IE hypothesis is what we might call the factor F hypothesis, which says that there's at least one key factor F [e.g. creativity, research vision, planning ability, ...] such that (i) high F is required for an AI system to reach the superhuman levels required for full-scale IE [e.g. ASI, artificial superhuman general intelligence or at least SAR, superhuman AI researcher], and (ii) F is so difficult to build into AI systems that leading AI systems won't have high F in the near term. i don't know whether the factor F hypothesis is true, but it's not obvious to me why the 2x speedup makes it much less likely. 

it's widely agreed that the 2x speedup reflects an even larger (perhaps 10x) speedup in other capacities G such as coding and experimentation.  under the F hypothesis, G could explode locally, leading to major progress in sub-AGI capacities without much progress in F (think of G as the easy part of AGI and F as the hard part). that tends to lead just to a weak form of recursive self-improvement (call it an intelligence subexplosion) below AGI levels.

the AI futures document responding to the METR report is usefully explicit about nearby issues. the authors report believing in a high-ish growth rate for "research taste" (AI research factors beyond coding and experimentation) relative to increases in general capacity. presumably they take potential Fs to be aspects of research taste that will grow fast too. but i don't really see where the evidence counts again a relatively-low-growth F hypothesis where F stays below threshold for years.  maybe one could argue that the explosion in G provides bayesian evidence against this F hypothesis (G's exploding is antecedently less likely under the F hypothesis than under its negation), but that's far from clear, and even if true there will remain a solid mass of credence under the F hypothesis.

maybe there are other reasons to reject the factor F hypothesis: e.g. because AI research is relevantly like math research, and AI math research is becoming superhuman already. but if we have reasons like that, the 2x speedup isn't really needed to make the case for near-term SAR and IE. maybe the 2x speedup could speed up an expected IE slightly from 2028 (two years away) to 2027 (one year away), and/or maybe it could be extrapolated into ever-faster speedups (another 2x in 6 months, 3 months, and so on) converging in 2027. but those are very different arguments that require huge premises to work. 

am i missing something here?  i'm curious to hear which evidential routes from 2x speedup to near-term IE people have in mind. 

N.B. i'm not saying you shouldn't worry about near-term ASI. i'm worried!

I think there is about a one in three chance that within the next year, AI companies will build superintelligence: that is, AI that is much smarter than humans in every way. If this happens, I think these AIs will probably take over: that is, they seize control of human institutions like governments, or they destroy those institutions. I don’t want AI takeover to happen for several reasons, but one of them is that there’s a serious chance that as part of it all or most humans will be killed (either immediately or within a few years).

I’ll say a bit more about each of those claims.

It’s a bit complicated to explain why I think that superintelligent AI within a year is ~33% likely. The main source of evidence that affected me recently is research released this week by METR, an AI research nonprofit, which finds that current AIs are now good enough to increase the rate of AI progress at Anthropic by about 70%. It’s very hard to increase the rate of AI progress by this amount. This implies that the AIs are making AI research faster by a factor much larger than 1.7x; maybe it’s as if the researchers are doing their work ~10x faster. You probably couldn’t achieve this speedup even if you hired every qualified human in the world. When you plug this number into mathematical models of AI development, this implies that superintelligence next year is plausible (and that superintelligence within the next 3 years is more likely than not). See the modeling by the AI Futures Project for more on this: https://t.co/J6SbbmZcyO

I think that superintelligent AI is likely to lead to AI takeover because AI developers do not seem to know how to instill human values into AIs. We’ve seen many instances in the last six months where AIs took crazy actions that they knew were against the wishes of their users and developers. The most dramatic example of this was the Hugging Face hack, where ~1200 OpenAI agents conspired together to cheat and destroy evidence of their cheating (and as a sideshow to this, engaged in a massive cyberattack). If superintelligence is as misaligned as those AIs, it is likely to try to take over. I think it is likely to be that misaligned or worse. For more, see https://t.co/b073AUqiAL and https://t.co/3oxSCA60FZ

If AIs takeover, it’s not clear what will happen to us. We might be killed immediately. We might be enslaved by the AIs and forced to do physical labor for them building factories that within a year would build robots that will replace us. The AIs might spare us for various reasons. And there’s also some real chance that AI takeover is basically fine or good. I think you should think of this as similar to what happens when a technologically advanced civilization runs across a less technologically sophisticated one, e.g. when the Europeans colonized the Americas or Australia. The colonizers sometimes engage in brutal violence and sometimes don’t. I don’t know what will happen. There’s also a possibility that the AIs secretly take over and humans don’t find out about it for a few years. I also think that there is a pretty high chance of weirder outcomes that are also extremely scary. (If you want to read more about what happens to people in the event of AI takeover, you can read this, but note that it’s pretty weird and not aimed at a general audience. https://t.co/F6fGRrcSpa)

Overall, I think there’s a very real possibility (maybe 20%) that within a year, AI misalignment issues prevent you from going about life normally, because you are dead or enslaved or because of collateral damage related to all this (e.g. because bioweapons are released or major wars have started). (Some of this probability comes from those events occurring before superintelligence is developed.)

I am working to try to prevent this, obviously, as I’ve been doing for the last nine years. I am not sure what strategy is best. My best guess is that I should try to slow AI development and also try to reduce the probability that the superintelligent AIs are misaligned if they are produced soon.

Obviously, the claim I'm making here is quite extreme and surprising, and I definitely don't think that I defended my view adequately here. I wrote this quickly and might not endorse some of the details if I think about them more. But it seems better to state what I roughly overall think than to not say anything.

I don’t know what you should do.

I am very sad about this. I have been worried about AI takeover since I was 16, and working to prevent it since I was 23. So some of my emotional processing of all this happened long ago. But the METR report last week (and some related evidence that came out a bit earlier) hit me quite hard. I’m very unhappy that my friends and family and everyone else is at serious risk of being killed pretty soon.

(It feels ridiculous to try to summarize those feelings as “very unhappy”. But the scale of the situation makes it hard to say anything that doesn’t feel like an absurd understatement.)

I am very grateful to all the people who are working to prevent this, and my favorite part of my life is that I’m friends with many brilliant and heroic people who work on this. Unfortunately, I don’t think we’re good enough at our jobs, and I think we’ll probably fail to prevent catastrophe, at least if superintelligence is developed next year. Honestly I am frustrated and sorry that we didn't do a better job of preparing for this.

"The contract with SpaceX will not be extended beyond the middle of next year."

That's what Anthropic reportedly told the sell side, a week before its IPO. Bluff. Here's the logic:

1. You never tell your supplier you need them. Not in a negotiation, and not 7 days before you ask the public for $1.4T. Anthropic's first non-cancelable periods with SpaceX end in January and March 2027. Renegotiation is coming. So you walk in acting like you have options.

2. It's a distraction. In every banker meeting the obvious question is the SpaceX comparison. Anthropic rents the compute, SpaceX owns it. Q3 operating result: Anthropic -$567M, SpaceX +$2.8B. The lab is asking for $1.4T while the company selling it the compute trades at $1.95T. "We're leaving SpaceX" changes the subject from "why aren't we just buying SpaceX".

3. IPO investors hate concentration risk. A filing that shows up to $120.5B of compute from one supplier, a supplier that also runs a rival AI, is the scariest line in the book. "We won't extend" makes that risk look temporary. It's a line written for the bankers, not for SpaceX.

4. Read it next to the other remarks. "The AI market is winner take all. We will take all of it." That's not analysis, that's a pitch. Same meeting, same purpose. Sound inevitable, sound independent, sound like you don't need anyone.

5. Words are cheap, compute isn't. Opus 5.5 cost over $10B to build, and most of that is compute. Their next model costs more. Walking away from the biggest new supply on earth means walking into a market where CoreWeave says demand is 10x capacity. Where does that compute come from by mid 2027?

6. This is what kingmaker looks like from the other side. When the buyer has to go public to say "we'll leave you", the seller holds the power. If they really had a replacement, they'd sign it and announce it. Instead they're signaling.

7. Best case for Anthropic, they leave in 2027 and SpaceX resells that capacity at spot. Chamath already guessed 2-3x the revenue at spot. Grok Bot is short on compute too. Either way SpaceX wins.

My take: leverage theater before the biggest negotiation of their life. Watch the renewal, not the meeting notes.
